title: Found out, heard, assumed
seoTitle: Turkmen -ypdyr, eken and -dyr: what you heard
intro: Turkmen often shows **how you know** what you say. Did you see it happen? Then the plain past: *Ol geldi*. Did you find it out afterwards, from what it left behind, or hear it from someone? Then `-(Y)pdYr`: *Ol gelipdir*. You met `-(Y)pdYr` for **he** and **they** in [A2 unit 2](a2-u02); this unit gives it in every person, with its negative and questions, and sets it beside `-dY` in short scenes. Then come *eken* after verbs (*Ol geljek eken*, he's coming, I hear) and `-dYr` for a confident guess (*Ol öýdedir*, he must be at home).

blocks.text: `-(Y)pdYr` tells an action you didn't witness: you know it from its result, or someone told you. Build it from `-(Y)p` and `-dYr`, then add the endings of **to be**, as in *talypdyryn* ([A1 unit 3](a1-u03)): *gelipdirin*, *gelipdir*, *gelipdiris*. One person is different: **you**. There is no `-dYr` with *sen* and *siz*; the ending goes straight onto `-(Y)p`: *gelipsiň*, *gelipsiňiz*.

rows.en: he or she has come (I see, I hear)
he or she has read (I see, I hear)

blocks.text: **About yourself, about the person in front of you.** Why would you say you did something without knowing it? Because you have only just realized it: you wake up on the bus at the last stop, *Men uklapdyryn!*, I've fallen asleep! Or you see a mistake: *Men ýalňyşypdyryn*, I was wrong, I see now. With **you**, it is often surprise at what you see: *Sen uly bolupsyň!*, you've grown up! *Sen üýtgäpsiň!*, you've changed!

items.en: I've fallen asleep on the bus!
I was wrong, I see now.
You've grown up!
You've come early!
We've taken the wrong road, it seems.

blocks.text: **Not.** The negative is built on `-mAn`, the negative of `-(Y)p` ([B1 unit 1](b1-u01)), and here **you** keeps `-dYr`: *gelmändirin, gelmändirsiň, gelmändir*. *Ol entek gelmändir*, he hasn't come yet, it seems.

rows.en: he or she hasn't come (it seems)

blocks.text: **Questions.** The particle goes at the end, *gelipdirmi?*, except with **you**, where it comes before the ending: *gelipmisiň?*, *gelipmisiňiz?* (the same order as *talypmysyň?*, [A1 unit 4](a1-u04)). Negative: *gelmänmisiň?*, *gelmändirmi?*

rows.en: Has he or she come, then?
Have you come, then? (plural or polite)

blocks.title: No -dYr with you
blocks.text: *gelipsiň*, not `gelipdirsiň`; *gelipsiňiz*, not `gelipdirsiňiz`. But in the negative **you** has it: *gelmändirsiň*. And keep the *p*: *gelipdir* (has come, I see), *gelipdi* (had come, [B1 unit 1](b1-u01)).

sections.title: Saw it or found out? -dY or -(Y)pdYr

blocks.text: English says **it snowed** in both of the scenes below. Turkmen doesn't. If you saw it, or simply state it as a fact you know, use the plain past `-dY`. If you found it out afterwards from its result, heard it from someone, or worked it out, use `-(Y)pdYr`. Read each pair and the note on what the speaker saw.

items.en: It snowed in the night.
items.note: You were awake and watched it fall.

items.en: It snowed in the night!
items.note: You wake up and everything outside is white.

items.en: My little brother broke the glass.
items.note: You saw him knock it off the table.

items.en: Someone has broken the glass.
items.note: You come in and find the pieces on the floor.

items.en: Merjen went to Mary.
items.note: You saw her off at the station.

items.en: Merjen has gone to Mary.
items.note: Her neighbour has just told you.

items.en: I went to sleep early yesterday.
I've fallen asleep!
items.note: You wake up at the last stop of the bus.

items.en: Mum made palaw.
items.note: You were in the kitchen with her.

items.en: Mum has made palaw!
items.note: You come home and smell it.

blocks.text: **News and stories.** When you pass on news you heard, `-(Y)pdYr` is the natural choice: *Eşitdiňmi? Merdan öýlenipdir!*, have you heard? Merdan has got married! The same holds for events long ago that nobody alive saw: writing about history often tells them in `-(Y)pdYr`, *Bu ýerde gadymy bir şäher bolupdyr*, there was an ancient city here. And folk tales are told this way from beginning to end ([A2 unit 2](a2-u02)).

**Switching in one breath.** A speaker can move from what they saw to what they found out: *Men oňa jaň etdim. Ol eýýäm gidipdir*, I called him (I did it); he had already left, it turned out (I learned it on the phone).

lines.en: Have you heard? Batyr has moved to Ashgabat.

lines.tk: Hawa, bilýärin. Men oňa kömek etdim.
lines.en: Yes, I know. I helped him.

lines.tk: Biz geçen şenbe onuň goşlaryny maşyna ýükledik.
lines.en: Last Saturday we loaded his things into the car.

lines.tk: Bir dostum aýtdy: ol täze iş tapypdyr. Şeýlemi?
lines.en: A friend of mine said he's found a new job. Is that so?
I don't know about that. He didn't tell me.

blocks.text: Aýna only heard the news, so she says *göçüpdir* and *tapypdyr*. Merdan was there, so for him it is *kömek etdim* and *ýükledik*.

blocks.title: Ask yourself: did I see it?
blocks.text: Yes, or it's simply what I know: `-dY`. No, I see the result, I was told, or I've worked it out: `-(Y)pdYr`. When in doubt about something you didn't witness, `-(Y)pdYr` is the safer choice.

In [A2 unit 2](a2-u02) *eken* followed a noun or an adjective: *Ol mugallym eken*, he's a teacher, it turns out. To report an **action** you have found out or heard about, *eken* follows a verb form, and which form depends on the time of the action:

blocks.caption: *eken* after a verb
head: Form
Example
Meaning
rows: She works, it turns out (or: she's working).
He came, it turns out (or: he had come).
He has to come, it seems.

blocks.text: Two of these forms are new. `-ýAn` is like `-ýAr` with *n* in place of *r*: *gelýän*, *okaýan*, *işleýän*. `-An` is the form you know from inside `-AndA` ([A2 unit 11](a2-u11)): *gel-en-de*, so *gelen*, *okan*, *işlän*. On their own they are participles, which describe nouns, and come in [B1 unit 5](b1-u05); here you only need them before *eken*. `-jAk` and `-mAlY` you know.

items.tk: Ol her gün işe pyýada gidýän eken.
items.seg: Ol her gün iş|e pyýada gid|ýän eken.
items.en: She walks to work every day, it turns out.
They've moved to Mary, it turns out.
The guests are coming tomorrow, I hear.
Merdan has to come at eight, it seems.
Aýna is getting married, I hear.

blocks.text: **Not.** The negative goes into the verb form: *gelmeýän eken* (doesn't come, it turns out), *gelmejek eken* (isn't coming, I hear), *gelmeli däl eken* (doesn't have to come). For `-An` the negative is *-mAdYk*: *Ol gelmedik eken*, he didn't come, it turns out.

**I and you.** *eken* takes the past endings, with a linking vowel: *ekenim*, *ekeniň*. *Men ýalňyşan ekenim*, I was wrong, it turns out; *Sen hem gelýän ekeniň!*, so you're coming too! In the plural you will see *ekenik*, *ekeniňiz*, and *ekenler* for **they**.

rows.en: he or she is coming, it turns out
you're coming, it turns out (plural or polite)

blocks.text: **`-(Y)pdYr` or `-An eken`?** Both tell what you didn't see. `-(Y)pdYr` is the everyday way to pass on news or what a result shows: *Ol gelipdir*. `-An eken` puts the weight on your discovery, often that the facts are not what you thought: *Men oňa jaň etjekdim, ýöne ol eýýäm gelen eken*, I was going to call him, but he had already come, as it turned out.

blocks.title: A separate word, and no -dY
blocks.text: *eken* is written apart: *gelen eken*, not `geleneken`. Nothing in `-dY` comes before it: *gelen eken*, not `gelipdi eken`.

sections.title: Must be, probably: -dYr for a guess

blocks.text: In [A1 unit 3](a1-u03) you met `-dYr` on nouns as a careful **is**: *Ol mugallymdyr*. In everyday speech the same ending very often marks a confident guess: *Ol öýdedir*, he must be at home, he's probably at home. Words like *megerem* and *ähtimal* (probably) or *belki* (maybe) make the guess clear: *Megerem, ol öýdedir.*

With **you**, `-dYr` takes the endings of **to be**, as in A1's formal *talypdyrsyň*: *Siz ýadawdyrsyňyz*, you must be tired. For **probably not**, `-dYr` goes on *däl*: *Ol öýde däldir*, he's probably not at home.

**Guessing about actions.** Put `-dYr` after the three verb forms of the last section: after `-An` for what has probably happened, after `-ýAn` for what is probably going on, after `-jAk` for what will probably happen.

blocks.caption: `-dYr` for a guess
head: Form
Example
Meaning
rows: He must have arrived by now.

items.en: They're probably on the way.
You must be tired; sit down.
He's not answering his phone. He must be sleeping.

items.tk: Sagat ýedi boldy. Merdan eýýäm öýe gelendir.
items.seg: Sagat ýedi bol|dy. Merdan eýýäm öý|e gel|en|dir.
items.en: It's seven o'clock. Merdan must have got home by now.
Probably he'll come tomorrow.

items.tk: Aýna öýde däldir, onuň maşyny bu ýerde ýok.
items.seg: Aýna öý|de däl|dir, on|uň maşyn|y bu ýer|de ýok.
items.en: Aýna can't be at home; her car isn't here.

blocks.title: Three ways of knowing
blocks.text: Saw it: *Ol geldi*. Found it out or heard it: *Ol gelipdir*, *Ol gelen eken*. Guessing: *Ol gelendir*. Same event, three different ways of knowing about it.

blocks.title: Guess or evidence: gelendir, gelipdir
blocks.text: One letter apart again. *gelipdir* rests on evidence: you saw his shoes, someone told you. *gelendir* is a guess from what usually happens: it's late, so he must have come.

summary: `-(Y)pdYr` in every person: *gelipdirin, gelipsiň, gelipdir, gelipdiris, gelipsiňiz, gelipdirler*; no `-dYr` with **you**.
`-dY` for what you saw or simply know; `-(Y)pdYr` for what you found out from a result, heard, or worked out.
*eken* after a verb: *gelýän eken* (now, usually), *gelen eken* (it happened), *geljek eken* (it will), *gelmeli eken* (it has to); *ekenim*, *ekeniň* for **I** and **you**.
`-dYr` for a guess: *Ol öýdedir*, *Siz ýadawdyrsyňyz*, *gelendir*, *işleýändir*, *geljekdir*; with *megerem*, *ähtimal*.
Saw it: *geldi*; found out: *gelipdir*, *gelen eken*; guessing: *gelendir*.
